title: Axe and hatchet care: sharpening, cold steel and swinging safely
summary: Keep an axe or hatchet sharp with a file and stone, in the convex shape it came with, on a tight handle. The injuries come from glancing blows off a dull or cold, brittle edge, a cluttered swing zone, and heads that fly off loose handles.

steps.text: Check the axe before the first swing: the head can't move on the handle, the wedge is in place, and there are no cracks in the handle just below the head (where handles break) or in the head itself (CCOHS general, Ax Manual ch9, ch13). The full checklist is in Checking a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge.
steps.warn: A loose, splintered or cracked handle can let the head fly off and hit you or someone near you (OSHA 3080).

steps.text: In hard frost, warm the head before you start: with the bit in its sheath or turned away from your body, tuck it under your arm inside your coat, or chop slowly for a few minutes so friction warms it (Ax Manual ch11, AATG use). Don't put it on the stove or in the fire: too much heat ruins the temper (Ax Manual ch8).
steps.warn: Cold steel is brittle and can chip or break: don't drive a cold axe into knots or frozen wood (Ax Manual ch11).

steps.text: Clear everything you could hit with the axe at full stretch all the way round you, overhead and behind, and keep other people well back (Ax Manual ch11, Fiskars firewood). Stamp down or clear snow and ice so your footing is firm and level (Ax Manual ch11 asks for good footing and a firm stance). Chop with someone within call if you can: the Forest Service says it is best not to chop alone (Ax Manual ch11).
steps.warn: Even a twig can deflect a blow, and split pieces can fly metres (Ax Manual ch11, Fiskars firewood).

steps.text: Put on safety glasses or goggles and stout leather boots at least 20 cm (8 in) high; gloves if they help your grip (AATG use, Ax Manual ch11).
Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart, weight even, and take a gentle first swing to judge your reach (AATG use).

Split on a solid chopping block rather than the ground, so a miss goes into wood. Start on an existing crack, swing straight down, and bend your knees a little as the bit lands (Fiskars firewood, AATG use, Ax Manual ch11).
steps.warn: If the bit sticks, rap the end of the handle down with your palm or finish with wedges. Levering it out crushes the wood just under the head, where handles break (AATG use, Ax Manual ch9).

steps.text: To sharpen, clamp the axe at about elbow height with the head out over the bench edge. A wooden jig holds the head without crushing the eye the way a tight vise can (Ax Manual ch7, ch8, ch9).

Fit a tight handle and a hand guard to the file, and wear gloves, at least on the hand near the edge: cut-resistant if you have them, heavy leather if not (Ax Manual ch8 accepts either, Council sharpen says heavy leather, Ax Manual ch7 for the guard). Leather isn't rated as cut-resistant (see the sharp hazard card), so keep your hand behind the guard.
steps.warn: A file with a loose handle or none can drive its tang into your palm if it slips (Ax Manual ch7).

steps.text: Push the file from the edge back toward the eye and lift it on the return. Work a fan shape about 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) back at the middle, and leave the toe and heel a little thicker (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch8, Council sharpen).
Turn the axe and file the other side the same way until the burr moves back across. Check both sides with a gauge cut to about 25 degrees (AATG hanging, Council sharpen).

Hone with the coarse side of an axe stone, then the fine side, in small circles toward the edge, with oil or water as the stone needs, until the burr is gone (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch8, Gränsfors sharpening).
steps.warn: Keep a high-speed dry grinder off the edge: it draws the temper. Steel that turns blue or purple has lost its hardness there (Council sharpen, Ax Manual ch8).

steps.text: Wipe the head and give it a light coat of oil or wax; rub linseed oil into the handle (Ax Manual ch9, ch12).
steps.warn: Linseed-oil rags can heat up and catch fire on their own: dry them spread out outdoors or keep them under water (Ax Manual ch9, AATG hanging).

steps.text: Sheath the axe to carry it, hold it near the head with the edge down, on the downhill side. Store it dry, but not beside the stove, where the handle shrinks (AATG use, Ax Manual ch11, ch12).
If the head works loose, stop and drive the wooden wedge further or fit a thicker one; don't soak it in water (Ax Manual ch12). For a new handle see Re-handling an axe, hammer, maul or file.

notes:
## What a working axe needs
A sharp edge with the right shape behind it, a head that can't move on the handle, a sound handle, and a sheath. A dull axe is the dangerous one: it glances off the wood instead of biting (AATG use, Ax Manual ch8). Check a found axe or hatchet with [Checking a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge](#guides/test_striking_tools) before the first swing; a loose or cracked one goes to [Re-handling an axe, hammer, maul or file](#guides/repair_tool_handle).

## Cold steel
An axe head is brittle in hard cold and can chip or break if you drive it into knots or frozen wood straight from the shed (Ax Manual ch11). Warm it first: with the bit sheathed or turned away from your body, tuck the head under your arm inside your coat, or chop slowly for a couple of minutes so friction warms it (Ax Manual ch11, AATG use). Don't put it on the stove or in the fire: too much heat ruins the temper (Ax Manual ch8). A thin, flat-ground edge is the most likely to bend or break on a hard knot or frozen wood; a convex edge is tougher (Ax Manual ch8). Frozen rounds split best with a maul or wedges (Penn State heating), but the Forest Service says not to chop knots or frozen wood with a cold axe: warm the tool first and use a maul or wedges rather than a thin-edged axe (Ax Manual ch11, ch8).

Wood heat brings its own winter problem: an axe kept beside the stove gets a handle that dries and shrinks in the eye, and the head works loose. Keep it somewhere dry but not hot, ideally in the same conditions you use it in, such as an unheated shed (Ax Manual ch12, Gränsfors care).

## The swing zone and stance
- **Clear the circle.** With the area clear, you should be able to swing the axe all the way round you. Clear everything in the arc, behind you too: even small twigs deflect a blow (Ax Manual ch11, AATG use).
- **People.** Keep the work area clear of other people; split pieces can fly metres (Ax Manual ch11, Fiskars firewood). Don't chop alone if you can help it: the Forest Service says it is best not to, and some national forests forbid their crews to (Ax Manual ch11). If you must, tell someone where you are and when you'll be back.
- **Feet.** About shoulder width, weight even, footing firm and as level as you can get it. Take a gentle first swing to judge your reach (AATG use). For splitting, Fiskars says to stand with your feet well apart: a wide stance keeps your legs out of the way if the blade slips past the block (Fiskars firewood). When you move, move your feet and body together (Ax Manual ch11).
- **Knees.** Bend them a little as the axe lands. With bent knees the axe is never lined up with your legs, and a glancing blow falls to the side. This is for downward swings onto a log from overhead; on a horizontal cut, place your feet so the bit lands far enough in front of you that it can't reach them (Ax Manual ch11). When cutting a log on the ground from beside it, keep the handle level with the ground as it lands; when limbing, never let the head drop below your hands (AATG use).
- **Dress.** Safety glasses or goggles (in Canada, look for the CSA mark; CCOHS lists hammering and chipping under flying-object hazards: CCOHS eyes) and stout leather boots at least 20 cm (8 in) high (AATG use, Ax Manual ch11). Gloves help on a splitting pile but can go slick in rain and cost you your grip (AATG use, Ax Manual ch11). A hard hat if anything can fall from above (AATG use). In winter, shed a layer before you start sweating and put it back on the moment you stop ([cold](#browse/hazards/cold)).

## Splitting
- Stand the round on end on a solid chopping block of hardwood. Penn State suggests a block 36 to 46 cm (14 to 18 in) high for splitting with a maul; Fiskars describes a hardwood block typically 60 to 80 cm high. Stand where a miss lands in the block, not past it (Penn State heating, Fiskars firewood).
- Stove lengths are usually 30 to 60 cm (12 to 24 in). Start on an existing crack; on knotty rounds, slab off the edges first. Swing straight down (AATG use).
- Split with a splitting axe or maul, which has a much steeper bit than a felling axe (AATG use). Levering a stuck axe out crushes the wood fibres where the handle meets the head, which is where handles break; this happens most when splitting firewood (Ax Manual ch9). If it sticks, rap the end of the handle down with your palm (AATG use), or leave it and finish with wedges.
- Drive steel wedges with a sledge whose face is bigger than the wedge's head, or with a maul whose poll the maker rates for it; never with an axe (Council right tool, Gränsfors care; see [Striking hardened tools](#guides/safety_struck_tools)).

## Edge and profile
Keep the shape the maker gave it: Gränsfors says to keep the original edge shape on both sides, because a wrongly ground axe slips more easily (Gränsfors sharpening). For a general working axe that means a convex profile that fattens smoothly back from the edge, not a flat wedge; a flat profile sticks in the wood and its edge rolls or chips more easily (Ax Manual ch8).

| Use | Edge angle | Source |
|---|---|---|
| General axe | About 25 degrees, slightly convex | AATG hanging, Council sharpen |
| Forest Service work axe | Bevel 17 to 21 degrees, with a microbevel of 25 to 32 degrees at the very edge | Ax Manual ch8 |
| Knots and limbing | Thicker: up to about 28 degrees on a double-bit's rough side | Ax Manual ch8 |

File back about 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) at the middle of the edge in a fan shape, and leave the toe and heel (the corners) a little thicker: they are unsupported and chip first (AATG hanging, Ax Manual ch8). A gauge cut from card, brass or thin wood to the angle you want shows when both sides match (AATG hanging); the Forest Service publishes gauge drawings (Ax Manual appB).

## Sharpening without a grinder
- **Hold it.** Clamp the axe to a bench at about elbow height with the head out over the edge, in good light (Ax Manual ch7, ch8). A wooden jig is better than a vise, which can crush the eye if done up too hard (Ax Manual ch9).
- **Guard your hand.** A guard on the file (a disc of leather, felt, fire hose or even card) and a tight handle on its tang, plus gloves at least on the hand near the edge. The Forest Service accepts cut-resistant or leather (Ax Manual ch8) and Council Tool says heavy leather (Council sharpen); leather isn't rated as cut-resistant ([sharp](#browse/hazards/sharp)), so use cut-resistant gloves if you have them and keep your hand behind the file's guard (Ax Manual ch7 on the guard). A file with no handle can drive its tang into your palm (Ax Manual ch7). Don't use a file as a pry bar: it is hard steel and snaps into sharp bits (Ax Manual ch7).
- **File into the edge.** Push from the edge back toward the eye and lift on the return; don't saw back and forth. Filing from the back toward the edge rolls the edge over (Ax Manual ch8, Council sharpen). Work both sides until the burr moves from one side to the other (AATG hanging).
- **Hone.** A round axe stone, coarse side then fine, in small circles toward the edge, with oil or water as the stone needs (AATG hanging, Gränsfors sharpening). A few strokes with a fine stone at the end of each working day keep the edge there (Ax Manual ch12).
- **Check.** With a light over your shoulder, look straight into the edge: a well-honed edge throws back no light (AATG hanging).

## Grinders
Not on the edge. A high-speed dry bench grinder draws the temper (Council sharpen, AATG hanging). If you reshape with a power sander, keep it off the edge, lift it often, and stop if the steel turns blue or purple: the hardness there is gone (Ax Manual ch8). Gränsfors takes out big nicks with a fine flat file or an emery wheel, does routine sharpening on a wet grinder or a stone, and says to cool the steel often (Gränsfors sharpening).

## Sheath, carry, store
- Sheath it whenever it travels. Leather or felt is best; a strip of fire hose makes a field sheath, but not for storage (it holds damp against the steel). No duct tape on the head (Ax Manual ch11). The Forest Service publishes drawings for leather sheaths you can make (Ax Manual appB).
- Carry a single-bit axe near the head, edge down, on the downhill side, so you can throw it clear if you trip. Never an unsheathed axe on your shoulder (AATG use, Ax Manual ch11).
- Hand it over with the blade turned away from both of you, and let go only when the other person says they have it (Ax Manual ch11).
- Never leave it lying with the edge exposed; sheath it, or lay it flat with the edge against something solid (AATG use).

## Head and handle care
- Wipe the head dry, then a light coat of oil, paste wax or petroleum jelly against rust (Ax Manual ch12, Gränsfors care).
- Raw or boiled linseed oil on the handle. When you hang a new handle, keep oil off the part that goes into the eye, where it lets the head slip; once it is hung, a few drops on the top of the handle and wedge stop them drying out (Ax Manual ch9). Linseed rags heat up and can catch fire by themselves: lay them out flat outdoors to dry or keep them under water ([self-heating](#browse/hazards/self_heating), Ax Manual ch9, AATG hanging).
- Watch the handle: small surface checks from drying are normal, but replace a cracked one (Ax Manual ch12).
- Loose head: don't soak it in water. The swollen wood is crushed in the eye and the head ends up looser once it dries (Ax Manual ch12). The older Forest Service manual says never to soak the handle except as a short-term emergency field tightening (AATG hanging), so treat it as a stopgap and re-wedge as soon as the wood has dried. Drive the wooden wedge further or fit a thicker one ([re-handling](#guides/repair_tool_handle)).

## Not with an axe
- Not as a wedge or a sledge, and don't strike it with a hammer or sledge (Council care, Gränsfors care). Hammering too hard on or with an axe can deform or break the eye (Gränsfors care).
- Not on steel wedges with the poll of a single-bit axe: the poll is not hardened, mushrooms, and its thin edges can break off when struck. Wooden or plastic wedges only (AATG use, Ax Manual ch13).
- Not into the ground; dig roots with a Pulaski or grub hoe (AATG use).
